newsitem.title: BOLIVIA: Bolivia finds bones that could be Che Guevara's.
newsitem.headline: Bolivia finds bones that could be Che Guevara's.

text.p: A team of Cubans, Argentines and Bolivians searching for the remains of Ernesto "Che" Guevara in Bolivia has found bones that "very probably" belong to the legendary revolutionary, Bolivian officials said on Wednesday.
"We are probably very close to the result we have been seeking," said Marcos Tufino, the official coordinating the dig near the town of Villagrande in the jungle highlands of southeastern Bolivia.

Searchers have found half a dozen skeletons and among them a bone with apparent traces of formaldehyde, making experts think it could belong to Guevara, who was captured by Bolivian troops in October 1967 and executed in a village schoolhouse.

"We now have six skeletons and one bone coloured slightly red ... probably a humerus, which according to one of the Cuban scientists could be one of Guevara's bones," Tufino told a news conference in La Paz.

"Various witnesses said Che's body was the only one of the guerrillas' bodies that was put in formaldehyde," said Tufino, adding that he hoped to have more details within hours but that definitive identification could take up to two weeks.

The Argentine-born leftist icon and hero of the Cuban revolution was trying to export Cuban communism to the South American mainland when he was captured -- wounded and starving -- on Oct. 8, 1967 and later shot by a soldier.

His body was put on display as a trophy before the world press, then buried at a secret site by his Bolivian military executioners. But first they chopped off his hands as proof that they had captured him.

Bolivia began the quest for Guevara's bones in December, 1995 after retired Gen. Mario Vargas Salinas broke two decades of military silence to say he could identify the spot where he ordered the burial of the guerrillas.

He failed to locate the exact spot and the search has since been repeatedly suspended and resumed, with excavations centering on an airstrip outside Vallegrande, 480 miles (775 km) southeast of La Paz. So far anthropologists have turned up three skeletons, at least one of which has been identified as belonging to Che Guevara's tiny revolutionary column.
The search was relaunched in May based on new evidence, including a truck driver who said he transported the bodies of Guevara and his comrades.
Impoverished Vallegrande has already declared Guevara's bones, when they are found, "the patrimony of the region" with plans to develop a local tourist industry around them.
But the Bolivian government plans to give them to Guevara's family, and his Cuban wife, Aleida March, has requested they be sent back to the Caribbean island for a final burial.
Born in Argentina where he studied medicine, Guevara made his fame as Fidel Castro's deputy in the Cuban revolution.

After victory in 1959 Castro made him president of the national bank, then industry minister, but Guevara gave it up to start a guerrilla campaign in Bolivia he hoped would spread across Latin America, but which was doomed from the outset.
